prompt.context: Your client is Parliament Denim, an iconic American jeans company. Over its 70-year history, Parliament has maintained steady financial success and earned a reputation for reliable jeanswear. One reason for its success is its internal production capabilities, a rarity in the denim industry. However, over the past 15 years, Parliament has experienced issues in operating its plant at capacity, as its Merchants and Designers have increasingly been going to externally sourced vendors for production. Parliament needs your help in reversing this trend to both avoid the excessive costs of plant down-time and to reclaim the competitive advantage that internal production offers.
prompt.question: How would you approach understanding why Parliament's plant is underutilized, and what would you recommend to reverse this trend?

clarifying_info.a: Parliament has operations globally, but we will focus only on the North American supply chain. The plant is in Mexico; products are sold primarily in the US.

clarifying_info.q: What channels does Parliament sell through?
clarifying_info.a: Parliament operates in three channels: Western (cowboys/farmers/rodeo), Mass (basic jeans — think Walmart or Target), and Modern (trendy).

clarifying_info.q: Has the plant invested in new equipment recently?
clarifying_info.a: New equipment has been sparingly invested in over the past 10 years.
Downtime costs $500k per plant per day.

exhibits.title: Consumer Poll: What Characteristics Do You Look For in Jeans?
exhibits.shows: A side-by-side consumer poll comparing 2008 and 2016 responses on desired jeans characteristics.

data.note: The chart shows relative importance of each characteristic in 2008 vs. 2016; Stretch has grown significantly in importance by 2016.

exhibits.title: Weekly Jeans Demand by Channel
exhibits.shows: A table showing weekly unit demand for fashionable jeans and basic jeans broken out by channel (Western, Mass, Modern).

data.note: Figures are per week. Total fashionable demand = 160,000/week; total basic demand = 290,000/week.

framework: Facilities: assess current plant capacity, equipment age, and utilization rates
Internal capabilities: evaluate whether existing machines and workforce can produce fashionable (stretch) jeans
Consumer demand: analyze how consumer preferences have shifted and whether internal production aligns with those preferences
Market forces: consider competitive pressure from external vendors — cost, speed, quality, and technology advantages
Cost structure: quantify the financial impact of downtime vs. outsourcing premiums

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1 — What does the consumer poll tell you, and why does it matter for Parliament?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that consumer preferences have shifted toward stretch/fashionable jeans between 2008 and 2016. A strong candidate connects this to Parliament's production problem: the plant was built for durable/basic jeans and likely lacks the cutting/sewing capabilities for stretch fabrics. This explains why Merchants and Designers increasingly go to external vendors who already have those capabilities. Candidate should then brainstorm why outsourcing is attractive for fashionable production: external vendors have newer technology, more accessible stretch fabrics, faster turnaround, better quality for new styles, and a flexible service model.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 — Calculate the plant's weekly production capacity for basic and fashionable jeans, and identify any capacity gaps.
questions.guidance: Candidate should subtract the 2-hour setup time per machine per day from the 18-hour operating day, leaving 16 productive hours. Then compute units per machine per day for each type. Sum across machines and across the 5-day week to get total weekly capacity. Compare to total weekly demand from Exhibit 2 to identify over/under capacity.

math.setup: Plant operates 18 hrs/day; setup time = 2 hrs/machine/day => 16 productive hrs/day. 5 days/week. Basic jeans: 30 sec/unit = 2 units/min = 120 units/hr. Fashionable jeans: 60 sec/unit = 1 unit/min = 60 units/hr. 35 basic machines; 15 fashionable machines.
steps: Basic capacity = 16 hrs/day x 5 days/week x 120 units/hr x 35 machines = 336,000 units/week
Fashionable capacity = 16 hrs/day x 5 days/week x 60 units/hr x 15 machines = 72,000 units/week
Fashionable gap = 72,000 - 160,000 = -88,000 units/week (undercapacity — 88,000 units must be outsourced)
math.answer: Basic jeans: 46,000 units/week surplus. Fashionable jeans: 88,000 units/week shortfall (must be outsourced). This explains plant underutilization — basic machines sit idle while fashionable demand overflows to external vendors.

questions.prompt: Parliament is considering investing $10M to convert some basic machines to fashionable ones. The renovated plant will meet 95% of basic demand and 85% of fashionable demand. Implementation requires 3 days of downtime. Calculate the NPV of this investment. (Assume a 12% discount rate, 2% demand growth rate, and 50 operating weeks/year.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should first calculate how much outsourcing Parliament currently pays (the 88k/week fashionable gap). Then calculate the residual outsourcing cost after renovation (5% of basic + 15% of fashionable unmet). Net annual savings = current outsourcing cost minus post-renovation outsourcing cost. Subtract one-time downtime cost in year 1. Apply perpetuity-with-growth formula (Gordon Growth) for NPV. Candidate should note that the project also solves the underutilization issue for basic machines.

math.setup: Outsourcing premium = $1.50/garment. Current outsourcing = 88,000 fashionable units/week (plant cannot produce). Post-renovation unmet demand: basic = 5% x 290,000 = 14,500/week; fashionable = 15% x 160,000 = 24,000/week. 50 weeks/year. Downtime = 3 days x $500k/day = $1.5M one-time cost in year 1. Discount rate r = 12%, growth rate g = 2%.
steps: Current annual outsourcing cost = 88,000 units/week x 50 weeks x $1.50 = $6,600,000/year
NPV = (FCF / (r - g)) - initial investment - downtime cost
math.answer: NPV ≈ $25.5M. The project is financially attractive. Break-even occurs between years 3-4.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might it be easier for Merchants and Designers to go to external vendors for fashionable/stretch jean production rather than use Parliament's internal plant?

categories.name: Technology & Equipment
ideas: External vendors have newer cutting and sewing machines suited for stretch fabrics
Parliament's aging equipment (sparse investment over 10 years) cannot handle new fabric types
Faster technology refresh cycles at third-party specialists

categories.name: Fabric & Materials Access
ideas: External vendors have established relationships with stretch-fabric suppliers
Sourcing stretch materials through an external vendor is simpler than retooling internal supply chain

categories.name: Speed & Flexibility
ideas: Outsourced orders can be placed quickly without internal scheduling conflicts
Vendors can offer faster turnaround for trend-sensitive Modern channel
External partners can scale volume up or down more easily

categories.name: Quality & Expertise
ideas: Vendors specializing in fashionable denim have deeper expertise in construction techniques
External partners may offer higher quality finishes for stretch products

categories.name: Service Model
ideas: Working with an external vendor is a simpler transactional relationship
Internal production requires coordination across departments; external vendor simplifies the process

recommendation: Parliament should invest $10M to convert basic production machines to fashionable ones. The project generates an NPV of approximately $25.5M, which strongly justifies the investment. The renovated plant will meet 95% of basic demand and 85% of fashionable demand, significantly reducing the $6.6M/year in outsourcing premiums and resolving the long-standing underutilization problem.
risks: Consumer trends may shift again, reducing demand for fashionable jeans and undermining the investment thesis
Implementation may take longer than 3 days, increasing downtime costs beyond the $1.5M estimate
The NPV is calculated under perpetuity assumptions — Parliament will likely need to upgrade equipment again in the future
Declining costs of outsourcing could erode the savings advantage of internal production
Labor force disruption during the 3-day implementation could cause productivity issues
A downturn in the overall denim market could reduce total demand
next_steps: Liaise with labor leaders to plan the transition and manage any workforce concerns during downtime
Identify the specific types of machinery needed for fashionable (stretch) jean production
Work with the forecasting team to model how consumer preferences may continue to shift
Plan inventory buffer to cover the 3-day production downtime

Evaluate alternative options: (a) sell fashionable machines and fully outsource fashionable production, (b) divest internal production entirely, or (c) acquire an outsourcing partner that already has stretch-fabric capabilities
